Authors: K. P. Das; M. Logamithran; S. Pratyush; G. Manju
Author Affiliations: School of Computer Science and Engineering (SCOPE), Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India; School of Computer Science and Engineering (SCOPE), Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India; School of Electronics Engineering (SENSE), Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India; School of Computer Science and Engineering (SCOPE), Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India
Publication Title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) is central to Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS), but existing solutions trade inspection depth for throughput. Snort and Suricata provide rich rule semantics but incur kernel-to-user copies; eBPF filters are fast but historically lack capacity for large regular-expression (RE) rulesets. We present ZDPI, a zero-copy DPI system that resolves this tension by combining three innovations: 1) a user-space control plane that compiles RE rulesets into EC-compressed DFA transition tables via Thompson NFA construction, subset-DFA conversion, Hopcroft minimization, and equivalence-class (EC) byte compression; 2) a two-stage in-kernel data plane consisting of an Aho-Corasick (AC) pre-filter followed by selective per-pattern MFSA traversal, fully implemented as an eBPF/XDP program; and 3) use of BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARENA (Linux 6.10 +) for a zero-copy shared memory region between control and data planes, eliminating map-copy overhead and enabling multi-MB DFA tables previously impossible in BPF. The data plane performs deterministic regular-expression matching over the supported regex subset at the XDP hook. DFA matching guarantees  $O(n)$  worst-case time per input byte, providing inherent immunity to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) attacks. In XDP dataplane measurements, ZDPI achieves 14.2 Mpps on DNS-sized packets (approximately 33 bytes) at 71 ns per packet; the two-server AWS ENA scaling test reaches 377,000 pps in the controlled comparison. The configurations are reported separately; the ENA result gives a  $4.6\times $  throughput improvement over Suricata under identical algorithmic conditions (AC pre-filter plus per-rule verification), 2, $786\times $  faster rule compilation than iterative MFSA merging, and a memory footprint of only 4 KB for 30 rules. The AC+MFSA design delivers  $2.39\times $  higher throughput than parallel MFSA-only traversal at 500 rules with near-zero clean-traffic overhead. All comparisons are supported by Mann-Whitney U tests ( $p \lt 0.05$ ), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and run-to-run coefficients of variation below 1.2%. ZDPI passes 7,020 fuzz tests with zero crashes and achieves zero false positives on clean HTTP traffic.

Publication Title: 2025 21st International Conference on Network and Service Management (CNSM)
Abstract: This paper presents TimeLSB, a covert channel built on TCP timestamps using extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) technology. The channel encodes information by modifying the least significant bit of timestamp values through a CRC32-based scheme in the Linux kernel, while a passive receiver reconstructs the hidden message. We implement and evaluate this channel under a range of controlled network impairments, demonstrating that embedding covert bits does not significantly alter the behavior of normal TCP connections. The eBPF implementation introduces only on average 250 ns of processing overhead per packet, which corresponds to several million packets per second and is negligible compared to typical forwarding performance. Finally, we analyze detectability using the distinct-timestamp ratio, showing that while absolute values differ from prior work, the metric still provides a stable separation between covert and normal flows. These results highlight the practicality of an eBPFbased covert channel and provide defensive insights for network security operations.
